opus-5.5.text:
I think the core tension is that language and vision are fundamentally different kinds of signals. Language is something humans invented. It's already highly compressed, discrete, and semantically dense. Every token carries a lot of meaning, so next-token prediction on text gives you a very efficient path to something that looks like intelligence. Vision is not like that. Pixels are continuous, extremely high-dimensional, and full of redundancy. Most of what's in an image is, in some sense, noise relative to whatever task you care about. So you can't just copy the LLM recipe, tokenize everything, predict the next token, and expect the same magic.

What happens in practice with most multimodal LLMs today is that vision becomes a kind of plug-in. You take a pretrained vision encoder, often CLIP-style, map its features into the language model's embedding space, and let the LLM do the heavy lifting. That works surprisingly well on many benchmarks, but when we looked carefully, for example in our Cambrian work, we found that many of those benchmarks don't really require looking at the image. The language prior is strong enough that the model can often guess. So we may be overestimating how much visual understanding these systems actually have.

So I frame the challenge this way: is language the right interface, or the right bottleneck, for visual intelligence? I lean toward thinking it isn't, at least not by itself. Language is a very low-bandwidth description of the world. Humans and animals build rich perceptual and spatial representations long before, or entirely without, language. Things like spatial reasoning, understanding 3D structure, tracking objects over time, and predicting what happens next in the physical world are hard to fully capture in words.

That's why I think the next step isn't just bolting a better vision encoder onto an LLM. We need to take visual representation learning seriously on its own terms, through self-supervised learning, video, and world-model-style objectives where the model has to predict and understand the physical world, not just describe it. LLMs are a powerful tool, and I don't think we should throw them away. But if we want real perception, vision has to be a first-class citizen, not a translation layer feeding into a language model.

r001.rationale: The response discusses visual complexity, video, and tracking objects over time, but it does not raise how an LLM-based approach would cope with the high temporal rate of visual input.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that language is almost unfairly suited to the LLM recipe, and vision is not. Text is already a compressed, discrete, human-produced abstraction. Every token carries meaning because a person chose to write it. The internet gives you trillions of those tokens, and next-token prediction turns out to be a remarkably good objective for learning that structure.

Pixels are nothing like that. A raw image is a dense, continuous, highly redundant signal with no built-in notion of what matters. If you naively tokenize it and ask a model to predict the next patch, you spend enormous capacity modeling things like texture noise and lighting that have very little to do with understanding. So the first question is representation: what is the right unit of visual "meaning" that a sequence model can actually reason over? That is where things like ViT, self-supervised learning, and later tokenizer design all come in.

The second piece is that language supervision only gets you so far. Captions on the internet are sparse and noisy. They tell you a cat is on a sofa, but almost never tell you where exactly, how far away, or what is occluded. If you build perception purely by aligning images to text, you inherit the blind spots of the text, and you end up with models that talk fluently about images while being surprisingly bad at seeing. We saw this very directly in our Cambrian work: a lot of multimodal LLM benchmarks were essentially solvable with the language model alone, and once you control for that, the visual signal was weaker than everyone assumed.

So I frame it as two coupled problems. One is building a strong visual representation that is grounded in the world rather than in captions, which I think has to involve self-supervised or world-model-style objectives. The other is the integration: how you connect that representation to a language model so the reasoning capacity of the LLM is actually used on the visual content, instead of the LLM just guessing from priors.

And honestly, I think there is a third, more philosophical piece, which is that vision is not only an input modality. It is tied to acting in a physical world. Language models can get away with being passive because text is a world people already described for them. Visual intelligence probably cannot. That is why I am increasingly interested in whether the "LLM-style" scaling story is the whole story for vision, or whether something closer to a world model, trained on how the world changes, is the missing ingredient.

r001.rationale: The response discusses visual representation and the challenges of raw pixels, but it does not raise how an LLM-based approach would cope with vision’s high temporal input rate.

astra-6.text:
I think the first question is what we mean by an “LLM approach.” If we mean using a transformer to process visual information, that’s one thing. If we mean turning everything into a sequence and predicting the next token, that introduces a different set of assumptions.

Language already gives you a discrete representation. With vision, you have to decide what the tokens should represent and what information to preserve. A picture contains many things at once—objects, spatial relationships, textures—and what matters depends on the task. Describing a scene is different from precisely locating an object or understanding how it moves.

So I would frame the challenge as finding the right representation and learning objective for visual understanding. We can borrow a lot from language models, but we still have to ask whether the model is learning to perceive the world, and how we would measure that beyond its ability to produce a convincing description.

r001.rationale: The response discusses visual representations, tasks, and measurement, but does not raise how an LLM approach would handle the high temporal rate of visual input.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first question is: what do we mean by an “LLM approach”? If we mean that everything has to become a sequence of discrete tokens and we predict the next token, then vision presents some interesting challenges. Language already gives you a relatively compact, structured representation. An image contains a huge amount of information, and much of it may be irrelevant to the task. So deciding what the visual tokens should represent is already a big part of the problem.

There’s also a distinction between talking about an image and actually perceiving it. A model might give a very convincing description while still struggling to locate an object precisely or understand a spatial relationship. Fluency doesn’t necessarily tell us how good the underlying visual representation is.

So I would frame the challenge as learning a representation that preserves the visual information you need, and then finding the right interface between that representation and language. Next-token prediction is a powerful framework, but I wouldn’t assume that it automatically gives us all the capabilities we want from a visual system. That’s something we have to test.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the volume and representation of image information, but does not raise how an LLM approach would cope with the high temporal rate of visual input.
